body:
How the Green Revolution changed agriculture

The introduction of high-yielding varieties and modern agricultural inputs increased crop productivity in several parts of India. Wheat production recorded particularly important gains, followed by improvements in rice production. The country moved towards greater foodgrain self-sufficiency and became less dependent on imported foodgrains.

Higher agricultural production also increased the quantity of produce sold in the market. This marketed surplus supported commercial agricultural activity and provided more foodgrains for government procurement and public distribution.

Economic changes in rural areas

  • Higher productivity: More agricultural output could be obtained from cultivated land, especially where irrigation and improved inputs were available.
  • Commercialisation: Agriculture increasingly produced crops for the market as well as household consumption.
  • Growth of supporting industries: Demand increased for fertilizers, pesticides, tractors, pump sets, threshers, storage, transport and agricultural machinery.
  • Expansion of rural markets: Higher agricultural incomes in successful regions increased demand for consumer goods, services and agricultural equipment.
  • More intensive cultivation: Irrigation and shorter-duration crop varieties made multiple cropping possible in many areas.

Regional inequalities

The Green Revolution did not benefit every region equally. Its initial success depended heavily on irrigation, fertile soil, access to agricultural credit, electricity and the availability of modern inputs.

Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh experienced substantial benefits because they possessed favourable agricultural conditions and supporting infrastructure. Parts of Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu also benefited. In contrast, many rain-fed, drought-prone, hilly and economically backward regions experienced slower agricultural improvement.

This created a regional agricultural imbalance. States and districts with irrigation and supporting facilities could increase productivity more rapidly than areas dependent mainly on uncertain rainfall.

Social inequalities

The benefits were also uneven among farmers. Large farmers generally possessed more land, capital and access to credit. They could purchase improved seeds, fertilizers, machinery and irrigation equipment more easily. Consequently, they were often the earliest and largest beneficiaries of the new technology.

Small and marginal farmers could also benefit from higher productivity, but the initial investment and recurring cost of modern inputs created difficulties for those with limited resources. Tenant farmers and landless agricultural workers did not automatically share the gains received by landowners.

The employment effects were mixed. Multiple cropping and intensive cultivation increased labour demand during certain agricultural operations. However, tractors, mechanical threshers and harvesting equipment reduced the need for manual labour in some operations. The overall effect depended on the crop, region and level of mechanisation.

Environmental consequences

The intensive use of irrigation and chemical inputs also created environmental problems in some agricultural regions.

  • Groundwater depletion: Excessive pumping of groundwater lowered water tables in heavily irrigated regions.
  • Waterlogging: Poor drainage and excessive irrigation caused some agricultural land to become waterlogged.
  • Soil salinity: Accumulation of salts reduced the productivity of affected agricultural land.
  • Soil nutrient imbalance: Excessive dependence on selected chemical fertilizers affected soil health.
  • Chemical pollution: Improper use of pesticides and fertilizers affected soil and water quality.
  • Reduced crop diversity: Concentration on a limited number of high-yielding crops, particularly wheat and rice, reduced the relative importance of some traditional crops in certain regions.

Overall assessment

The Green Revolution increased foodgrain production and improved national food availability, but it did not eliminate rural poverty, unequal land ownership, regional disparities or environmental problems. Higher agricultural production alone could not guarantee that every household had access to adequate food.

Gujarat's contribution to rural transformation: The White Revolution

Gujarat provides an important example of rural economic transformation through cooperative dairying. This development is related to the broader transformation of rural India, but it is different from the Green Revolution.

The origin of the Anand cooperative model

The Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union was registered in Anand in December 1946. Its cooperative dairy products became widely known under the brand name Amul. The model enabled milk producers to organise collectively rather than depending entirely on private milk traders.

The cooperative system connected village milk producers with organised collection, processing and marketing facilities. Farmers could collectively supply milk, receive payments and participate in the management of their producer-owned institutions.

National Dairy Development Board

The National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) was established in 1965. It helped expand the Anand cooperative model to other parts of India. Dr. Verghese Kurien played a leading role in this development and is widely known as the Father of India's White Revolution.

Operation Flood

Operation Flood was launched in 1970 to increase milk production, connect milk producers with urban markets and expand dairy cooperatives across the country. It was implemented in 3 phases between 1970 and 1996.

The programme promoted organised milk procurement, processing, transportation and marketing. It strengthened the position of milk producers by connecting village-level cooperatives with larger dairy institutions and consumer markets.

The three-tier Anand Pattern

  • Village level: Dairy Cooperative Society, where milk producers become members and supply milk.
  • District level: Milk Union, responsible for processing, technical support and organised procurement from village societies.
  • State level: Federation, responsible for coordinating marketing and distribution across the State.

Green Revolution and White Revolution compared

FeatureGreen RevolutionWhite Revolution
Main focusFoodgrain production.Milk and dairy production.
Main approachHYV seeds, irrigation, fertilizers, pesticides and machinery.Producer-owned dairy cooperatives, milk collection, processing and marketing.
Important geographical connectionPunjab, Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh and other irrigated agricultural regions.Anand, Gujarat, through the cooperative dairy model.
Important people and institutionsM.S. Swaminathan, Norman Borlaug and agricultural research institutions.Verghese Kurien and the National Dairy Development Board.
Major resultHigher foodgrain productivity and food availability.Expansion of dairy production and organised rural milk marketing.

The Anand model demonstrates that rural development can occur through producer-owned institutions as well as technological improvement. It created a system through which small milk producers could collectively participate in processing and marketing, improving their access to organised markets.

Gujarat connection

Green Revolution refers primarily to higher foodgrain productivity through modern agricultural technology. White Revolution refers to the expansion of milk production through dairy development and cooperative institutions. Amul and the Anand Pattern belong to the White Revolution.

Prelims focus

  • The Green Revolution initially benefited irrigated and relatively prosperous agricultural regions more strongly.
  • Higher agricultural productivity increased marketed surplus and supported foodgrain procurement.
  • Groundwater depletion, waterlogging and soil salinity were important environmental consequences.
  • NDDB was established in 1965; Operation Flood began in 1970 and continued until 1996.
  • The Anand Pattern has village, district and State-level cooperative institutions.
  • Dr. Verghese Kurien is associated with the White Revolution.
  • Trap: Amul and Operation Flood are associated with dairy development, not the Green Revolution.

[Sources: NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class XI Economics, Chapter 2, Indian Economy 1950–1990, pp. 17–31; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class XII Geography, Chapter 5, Land Resources and Agriculture, pp. 40–59; National Dairy Development Board, Operation Flood, Anand Pattern and institutional history; NDDB, Verghese Kurien biography; Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union and Amul historical account. Online sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]

title: Green Revolution: Results, Inequality and Gujarat's Rural Transformation

body:
Meaning of food security

Food security means ensuring that all people have access to sufficient and nutritious food at all times. It is not enough for a country to produce large quantities of foodgrains. People must also be able to obtain and afford the food they need.

NCERT explains food security through 3 important dimensions:

  • Availability: Sufficient food must be available through domestic production, imports and government food stocks.
  • Accessibility: Food must be physically available and within reach of every person.
  • Affordability: People must have sufficient purchasing power to obtain adequate and nutritious food.

Food self-sufficiency and food security are different

Food self-sufficiency means that domestic production is sufficient to meet the country's food requirements. Food security additionally requires that individual households have the income, access and ability to obtain adequate food. A country may produce sufficient grain while poor households still experience hunger.

Hunger and food insecurity

Chronic hunger

Chronic hunger occurs when a person does not receive sufficient food over a long period. It is generally associated with persistent poverty, low income and inadequate purchasing power.

Seasonal hunger

Seasonal hunger occurs during particular periods of the year when employment and income are insufficient. Agricultural labourers may experience it between agricultural seasons when work opportunities decline.

Landless agricultural workers, marginal farmers, casual labourers, traditional artisans and households with irregular employment are particularly vulnerable to food insecurity. Women and children may also suffer from inadequate nutrition even when food is available within the household.

India's food management system

India developed a system of price support, government procurement, storage and public distribution to protect farmers and improve food availability for consumers.

Minimum Support Price

The Minimum Support Price (MSP) is a price announced by the government for specified agricultural crops. It provides farmers with a price-support mechanism when market prices fall. MSP announcements are generally made before the relevant sowing season so that farmers can consider price support while deciding what to cultivate.

The Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP) recommends MSPs after considering production costs, demand and supply, market prices, inter-crop price relationships and other relevant factors. The Union Government takes the final decision. CACP does not itself purchase crops or make the final MSP decision.

Food Corporation of India

The Food Corporation of India (FCI) was established on 14 January 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964. It became a major institution in India's food management system.

Its principal functions include:

  • Procurement of foodgrains from farmers through government procurement arrangements.
  • Storage and maintenance of foodgrain stocks.
  • Movement of foodgrains from surplus regions to deficit regions.
  • Distribution of foodgrains under government food-security programmes.

State procurement agencies also participate in purchasing and handling foodgrains. Government procurement is especially important for wheat and rice.

Buffer stocks

A buffer stock is a reserve of foodgrains maintained by the government to meet shortages, support the Public Distribution System, respond to emergencies and help stabilise foodgrain availability and prices.

When procurement is high, foodgrains can be added to government stocks. During shortages or increased requirements, stored foodgrains can be released for distribution. The buffer stock policy was formally introduced during the Fourth Five-Year Plan, 1969–1974.

Public Distribution System

The Public Distribution System (PDS) distributes essential commodities, particularly foodgrains, to households through a network of Fair Price Shops. It helps improve the accessibility and affordability of food.

The PDS developed from the rationing arrangements introduced during periods of scarcity. It was expanded during the 1960s. Initially, the system operated largely on a general basis rather than being restricted only to identified poor households.

The Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) was introduced in June 1997 to focus assistance on identified poor households. The Antyodaya Anna Yojana (AAY) was launched in December 2000 to provide additional support to the poorest households.

National Food Security Act, 2013

The National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) gave eligible households statutory foodgrain entitlements and strengthened the rights-based approach to food security.

The Act provides for coverage of up to:

  • 75% of the rural population.
  • 50% of the urban population.

It recognises 2 principal beneficiary categories:

  • Priority Households (PHH): Entitlement of 5 kg of foodgrains per person per month.
  • Antyodaya Anna Yojana households (AAY): Entitlement of 35 kg of foodgrains per household per month.

The coverage percentages are statutory maximum coverage limits, not a statement that every person in every State receives an identical ration card category. State and Union Territory governments identify eligible households within their respective coverage limits.

Responsibilities of the Union and State governments

  • Union Government: Responsible for foodgrain procurement arrangements, central storage, allocation to States and transportation up to designated delivery points.
  • State and Union Territory governments: Identify eligible households, issue ration cards, arrange distribution through Fair Price Shops and monitor delivery to beneficiaries.

How the food-security system works together

InstrumentMeaningContribution to food security
MSPGovernment-announced support price for specified crops.Provides price support to farmers.
ProcurementPurchase of eligible foodgrains by FCI and State agencies.Creates government stocks and supports farmers.
Buffer stockFoodgrains stored for future requirements.Helps manage shortages and supply requirements.
PDSDistribution through Fair Price Shops.Improves food accessibility and affordability.

Important distinction about MSP procurement

An MSP announcement does not mean that the government automatically purchases every farmer's entire production. Procurement depends on the crops covered, quality requirements, procurement arrangements, available centres and the marketable surplus offered for purchase. Government procurement has historically been concentrated particularly on wheat and rice in major surplus-producing regions.

Sugarcane is covered by a separate Fair and Remunerative Price (FRP) mechanism. It should not be confused with the 22-crop MSP framework.

Policy status at the 22 November 2026 content cutoff

The Union Government's official statement of 4 August 2026 reaffirmed the annual MSP framework for 22 mandated crops. The related procurement data covered 2021–2022 to 2025–2026, up to June 2026. The official crop classification comprises 14 kharif crops, 6 rabi crops and 2 commercial crops. Sugarcane is covered separately through FRP. Individual MSP rates are not reproduced here because they change annually.

Food security therefore depends on several connected arrangements. Higher agricultural production improves availability, MSP and procurement support agricultural producers, buffer stocks maintain reserves and the PDS helps households obtain food at affordable prices. However, adequate nutrition also requires a diverse diet, clean drinking water, sanitation and access to health services.

Prelims focus

  • Food security has 3 NCERT dimensions: availability, accessibility and affordability.
  • FCI was established on 14 January 1965 under the Food Corporations Act, 1964.
  • Agricultural Prices Commission was established in January 1965 and renamed CACP in March 1985.
  • Buffer stock policy was introduced during the Fourth Five-Year Plan, 1969–1974.
  • TPDS began in June 1997; Antyodaya Anna Yojana began in December 2000.
  • NFSA 2013: up to 75% rural and 50% urban coverage; PHH receives 5 kg per person per month and AAY households receive 35 kg per household per month.
  • Trap: MSP recommendation, government procurement, buffer stocks and PDS are different stages of the food-management system.

[Sources: NCERT, Economics, Class IX, Chapter 4, Food Security in India, pp. 42–53; Food Corporation of India, official history and Annual Report 2024–2025; Department of Food and Public Distribution, Public Distribution System history and Annual Report 2024–2025; Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices, official institutional history; National Food Security Act, 2013, Sections 3 and 10; Indian Economic Service, Arthapedia, Buffer Stock Policy; Government of India, official MSP policy statements dated 3 February 2026 and 4 August 2026. Online sources consulted on 22 November 2026.]
